title: Review: Greenhouse effect; Gas laws
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: B.3#c04 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; B.3#c01 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; B.2#c01 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; B.2#c07 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition. Questions: B.2#q08, B.2#q12, B.2#q14, B.2#q16, B.2#q18, B.3#q08, B.3#q11, B.3#q13, B.3#q16, B.3#q18, B.3#q14. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Avogadro constant (N_A)
items.clue: The number of particles per mole.

items.label: Pressure
items.clue: The perpendicular force on a surface per unit area.

items.label: Conservation of energy
items.clue: It cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred.

items.label: Albedo (α)
items.clue: The fraction of incident radiation that a planet or surface scatters back.

questions.stem: Sunlight of the same intensity falls on every part of a region of ocean. Cloud covers 30% of the region's area, and the cloud-covered part has an albedo of 0.60. The cloud-free 70% has an albedo of 0.06. What is the albedo of the region as a whole?
questions.explanation: Weight each albedo by the fraction of the incident power it receives: 0.30 × 0.60 + 0.70 × 0.06 = 0.180 + 0.042 = 0.222 ≈ 0.22.

questions.stem: The solar constant at Earth, at a mean distance of 1.50 × 10¹¹ m from the Sun, is 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻². Mars orbits the Sun at a mean distance of 2.28 × 10¹¹ m. What is the equivalent of the solar constant for Mars?
questions.explanation: The Sun's power spreads over a sphere of area 4πd², so S ∝ 1/d². S_Mars = 1.36 × 10³ × (1.50/2.28)² = 589 W m⁻².

questions.stem: Earth is modelled as a single black-body emitter with an albedo of 0.30, ignoring the greenhouse effect. The solar constant is 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻². Using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, estimate Earth's equilibrium temperature.
questions.explanation: Absorbed intensity = (1 − 0.30) × 1360/4 = 238 W m⁻² = σT⁴, so T = 255 K. This is about 33 K below Earth's observed mean surface temperature; the difference is the greenhouse effect.

questions.stem: Methane is released naturally from wetlands and also by human activity, for example livestock farming. Which statement about the absorption of infrared radiation by methane from these two sources is correct?

options.text: Only the methane from farming absorbs infrared; methane from wetlands is part of a natural balance.
Methane from farming absorbs more strongly, because it is released with pollutants that trap heat.
Neither absorbs much, since carbon dioxide is the only gas in air that absorbs infrared.
Methane from both sources absorbs infrared identically, as absorption depends on the molecule.

questions.stem: In a simple model, a greenhouse-gas molecule in its ground state has one excited vibrational energy level, 1.33 × 10⁻²⁰ J above the ground state. Infrared photons of wavelengths 10.0 μm, 15.0 μm and 20.0 μm fall on such molecules. Which photons can be absorbed? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)

options.text: The photons of 10.0 μm and 15.0 μm
Photons of all three wavelengths
None of these infrared photons
Only the photons of 15.0 μm

questions.explanation: E = hc/λ gives 1.99 × 10⁻²⁰ J, 1.33 × 10⁻²⁰ J and 9.95 × 10⁻²¹ J. Only the 15.0 μm photons have an energy equal to the gap between the levels, so only they are absorbed.

questions.stem: On a pressure–volume diagram (pressure on the vertical axis, volume on the horizontal axis), a fixed mass of ideal gas moves from state X to state Y along a horizontal straight line. At X the volume is 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ and the temperature is 27 °C; at Y the volume is 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³. What is the temperature at Y, and under what condition does the change X → Y take place?

options.text: 327 °C, at constant pressure
54 °C, at constant pressure
27 °C, at constant temperature
−123 °C, at constant pressure

questions.explanation: A horizontal line on a P–V diagram means the pressure is constant, so V/T is constant with T in kelvin. The volume doubles, so T doubles from 300 K to 600 K, which is 327 °C.

questions.stem: Two identical rigid containers are at the same temperature and the same pressure. One holds hydrogen (H₂) and the other holds carbon dioxide (CO₂). Both gases behave as ideal gases. How do the numbers of molecules in the two containers compare?

options.text: They are equal, as equal pressure, volume and temperature mean equal numbers.
There are more H₂ molecules, as smaller molecules leave room for more of them.
There are more CO₂ molecules, as the heavier gas is the larger amount of substance.
There are fewer CO₂ molecules, as each heavier molecule strikes the walls harder.

questions.explanation: PV = Nk_B T contains no property of the molecules, so equal P, V and T mean equal N. A CO₂ molecule is heavier, but at the same temperature it moves more slowly, and the two effects on pressure cancel.

questions.stem: A sample of helium at 300 K has a density of 0.160 kg m⁻³. The mean speed of its atoms is 1.26 × 10³ m s⁻¹, and the mean of the squares of their speeds is 1.87 × 10⁶ m² s⁻². Treat helium as an ideal gas. What is its pressure?
questions.explanation: In P = ⅓ρv², v² is the mean of the squared speeds, 1.87 × 10⁶ m² s⁻². P = ⅓ × 0.160 × 1.87 × 10⁶ = 9.97 × 10⁴ Pa.

questions.stem: A fixed mass of ideal monatomic gas is compressed slowly to half its volume while its temperature is kept constant. What happens to the internal energy U of the gas?

options.text: It increases, as the closer molecules store more intermolecular potential energy.
It does not change, as the temperature and so the mean kinetic energy are fixed.
It increases, because work is done on the gas while it is being compressed.
It doubles, because the pressure doubles and molecules hit the walls twice as often.

questions.explanation: For an ideal monatomic gas the internal energy is only the translational kinetic energy of the molecules, U = (3/2)Nk_B T. With N and T fixed, U is unchanged; the work done on the gas is transferred out of it thermally.

questions.stem: A real gas at a temperature a little above its boiling point is compressed to a high density. Its measured pressure is found to be lower than the value that PV = nRT predicts for the same n, V and T. Which is the best explanation?

options.text: The molecules take up part of the volume, which leaves less space for the gas and so lowers its pressure.
Collisions between real molecules are inelastic, so the molecules slow down and the pressure falls.
Attractive forces between the molecules pull those near a wall back, so they strike it with less momentum.
Near the boiling point the molecules have almost stopped moving, so few of them reach the walls.

questions.stem: A sealed, rigid container of ideal gas is heated. What happens to the pressure of the gas, and why?

options.text: It rises: the molecules expand when they are heated, so they strike the walls more often.
It stays the same: the number of molecules per unit volume has not changed at all.
It rises: faster molecules hit the walls more often, each with a greater change in momentum.
It rises: the molecules collide more often with one another, and so push harder on the walls.

questions.explanation: The volume and number of molecules are fixed, but heating raises the mean square speed. Faster molecules cross the container more often, so they strike each wall more frequently, and each collision reverses a larger momentum. Both effects raise the force per unit area.
